INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
The Retail Litigation Center, Inc. (“RLC”) is a
501(c)(6) nonprofit trade association that represents
national and regional retailers, including many of the
country’s largest and most innovative retailers, across
a breadth of retail verticals. The RLC is the only trade
organization solely dedicated to representing the retail industry in the courts. The RLC’s members employ millions of people throughout the United States,
provide goods and services to tens of millions more,
and account for hundreds of billions of dollars in annual sales. The RLC offers retail-industry perspectives to courts on important legal issues and highlights the industry-wide consequences of significant
cases. Since its founding in 2010, the RLC has filed
more than 250 amicus briefs on issues of importance
to the retail industry. Its amicus briefs have been
helpful to courts throughout the United States, as evidenced by citation to those briefs in numerous precedential opinions. See, e.g., South Dakota v. Wayfair,
Inc., 585 U.S. 162, 184 (2018); Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley
& Sons, Inc., 568 U.S. 519, 542-43 (2013); Chewy, Inc.
v. U.S. Dep’t of Lab., 69 F.4th 773, 777-78 (11th Cir.
2023); State v. Welch, 595 S.W.3d 615, 630 (Tenn.
2020).1
The RLC and its members have a significant interest in the outcome of this case. Virtually every major retailer has a website, and virtually every one of
those websites provides audiovisual content that is
freely available to visitors to the website. Customers
1

2
value and seek out such content, which can be accessed without a subscription, signing up, or making
a purchase.
But over the past four years, retailers have been
targeted with claims that they somehow violated the
Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988 (“VPPA”), 18
U.S.C. § 2710, merely because their websites contained some pre-recorded video content. Most of these
claims have been brought by a handful of plaintiffs’
firms—often using serial plaintiffs. These lawsuits exploit the $2,500 in statutory damages available under
the VPPA. They seek to expand the statute far beyond
its textual, contextual, and structural contours. Many
rest on the same expansive interpretation of who
counts as a “consumer” under the VPPA that Petitioner advances in this case.
RLC, its members, and the retail industry thus
have a strong interest in affirmance of the judgment
below. The Sixth Circuit properly held that a person
must rent, buy, or subscribe to video tapes or similar
audiovisual materials to be a ‘consumer’ under the
VPPA. That approach not only interprets the statute
correctly, but also provides needed clarity on the types
of customer relationships that implicate the VPPA.
And given the ubiquity of freely-available video content on retailers’ websites, Salazar’s contrary reading
of the statute would open the floodgates to abusive
VPPA litigation practices by permitting claims to advance even though they are wholly untethered to the
video-viewing privacy issues that Congress intended
to address.

3
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
Under the VPPA, a “consumer” is “any renter,
purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a
video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1).
The phrase “goods or services” cannot be read in a
vacuum, as the Sixth Circuit below and the D.C. Circuit have correctly held. The statute’s text, context,
and structure— including the interrelated definitions
of “video tape service provider” and “personally identifiable information”—are all focused on video tapes or
similar audiovisual materials. Thus, a “consumer” under the VPPA is likewise limited to people who rent,
buy, or subscribe to video tapes or similar audiovisual
materials (such as a person who rents a DVD or Blu-
Ray). See Paramount Br. 18-31.
RLC submits this brief to supply additional context underscoring the practical problems that would
flow from Salazar’s contrary interpretation. That interpretation makes the purchaser or renter of any
product—even retail products that are entirely unrelated to video content—a “consumer” under the VPPA.
There has already been a surge of VPPA litigation in
recent years, as some plaintiffs and their lawyers have
sought to leverage the VPPA’s nationwide coverage
and minimum statutory damages of $2,500 per violation. Salazar’s sweeping attempt to expand the scope
of the VPPA, if adopted, will no doubt lead to a new
flood of abusive claims under the statute.
This risk is particularly acute for retailers. Video
content is ubiquitous on retailers’ websites; customers
expect and desire video content, and retailers make
free video content available to provide visitors with
more information about the retailers’ stores, products,

4
and services. Additionally, most customers interact
with retailers through both brick-and-mortar stores
and websites, but the majority of retail sales still happen at brick-and-mortar stores. Nonetheless, under
Salazar’s approach, all of those in-store purchasers
who happen to visit the retailer’s website and encounter audiovisual content would become potential VPPA
plaintiffs.
Accordingly, the recent surge in VPPA lawsuits
will only get worse if the Court adopts Salazar’s interpretation. For decades after it was enacted, only a relative handful of VPPA claims were asserted. Starting
in 2022, however, serial plaintiffs and their counsel
began filing hundreds of similar lawsuits attempting
to expand the VPPA far beyond its intended contours
by pointing to the use of commonplace website technologies. (It is telling that Salazar himself is a plaintiff on both sides of the circuit split.)
Retailers were heavily targeted at the outset of
this surge, almost entirely by a small group of “tester”
plaintiffs who alleged that they had purchased a product from a retailer at some point in the past and then
subsequently watched a freely available video on the
same retailer’s website. Most of those lawsuits appear
to have been successful in coercing quick settlements,
even though the courts that reached the merits correctly concluded that the claims were implausible—
including because merely purchasing any product in
the past and then watching a website video does not
transform a plaintiff into a VPPA “consumer.”
If Salazar’s approach prevails, however, the inevitable result will be a new surge of similarly abusive
VPPA litigation, including against retailers whose
core business has little or nothing to do with selling or

5
delivering video content. That result is contrary to
both the text and structure of the statute.
The Court should affirm.
ARGUMENT
I. Petitioner’s Overreaching Interpretation
Of “Consumer” Threatens To Expose Retailers To Coercive VPPA Lawsuits.
The VPPA was not designed to be an omnibus Internet privacy statute—which is not surprising, given
that it was adopted well before the advent of the modern Internet. Instead, as the Third Circuit has put it ,
the VPPA “serves different purposes, and protects different constituencies, than other, broader privacy
laws.” In re Nickelodeon Consumer Priv. Litig., 827
F.3d 262, 288 (3d Cir. 2016).
Or, as this Court has explained in the context of
the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (a law of similar vintage), a statute should not be used “as an ‘agile
tool’” that automatically adapts to evolving technologies or circumstances. Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid, 592
U.S. 395, 408-09 (2021) (citation omitted) (rejecting
overbroad reading of the TCPA’s definition of an “automatic telephone dialing system”). Instead, statutes
must be given their “best reading” in light of their text
and context, even if the result is to limit the statute to
“senescent technology.” Id. at 409 (citation omitted).
Yet Salazar’s expansive reading of the VPPA
would stretch the statute far beyond its intended
reach. With respect to retailers in particular, virtually
every major national retailer offers some form of
online audiovisual content. And under Salazar’s interpretation of the VPPA, everyone who makes any purchase from such a retailer, whether online or at a

6
brick-and-mortar store—a pair of jeans, a coffee mug,
a box of cereal, or a tube of toothpaste—is a VPPA
“consumer.”
That interpretation would give the VPPA a
breathtaking sweep that reaches far more broadly
than the statute allows. And when coupled with the
VPPA’s nationwide coverage and $2,500 statutory
damages provision, Salazar’s interpretation, if accepted, would threaten retailers with massive potential exposure for alleged conduct that bears no resemblance to the conduct that Congress enacted the VPPA
to address.
Moreover, market realities make it difficult, if not
impossible, for retailers to avoid that risk. Audiovisual content is a critical part of retailers’ online presence. And even brick-and-mortar purchasers frequently visit retailers’ websites and watch video content about the retailer’s products or services, even if
they do not make a purchase online.
As a result, under Salazar’s interpretation retailers face potential VPPA claims from virtually all of
their website visitors, because any website visitor who
views a video on a retailer’s website and makes an entirely unrelated in-store purchase could conceivably
pursue a claim. The statute should not be interpreted
to permit such an incongruous result.
A. Retail customers desire, and retailers
routinely provide, digital video content.
Most major retailers have digital video content on
their websites to market their goods and brands.
That is simply a function of the modern Internet.
Videos are the most consumed and most popular type

7
of content on the internet, accounting for roughly 80%
of all web traffic. See Odysseas Garganas, Digital
Video Advertising: Breakthrough or Extension of TV
Advertising in the New Digital Media Landscape?,
Journal and Media (June 14, 2024),
https://doi.org/10.3390/journalmedia5020049.
Indeed, digital video content is ubiquitous across
websites of all kinds, including retail websites. Even
this Court has a video on its website (and sells goods
in its gift shop, which is linked on the Court’s main
website).2
Many retailers have added some form of freelyavailable digital video content to their websites. Digital audiovisual content on retail websites runs the
gamut from product demonstrations or overviews, to
how-to guides (such as assembly instruction videos),
to brand stories that highlight the retailer’s mission
or manufacturing processes. Visitors to the website
are not necessarily seeking out the video content in
particular—they may just be browsing or shopping
and encounter the videos as part of the enhanced experience that retailers offer and that customers have
come to expect.
A common characteristic of digital videos on retailers’ websites is that they “are aimed toward the
sale of [the retailer’s] products and are a marketing
tool to promote [the retailer’s] brand and website.”
Hernandez v. Container Store, Inc., 2024 WL 72657,
at *2 (C.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2024). In other words, the

in the shopping experience, even if they ultimately
buy the product in a store.3
In other words, the reality of modern shopping
habits demonstrates that customers primarily

purchase goods in a brick-and-mortar store, but frequently visit the same retailer’s website at some point
during the shopping experience. Under Salazar’s interpretation, each of these customers is a potential
VPPA “consumer.”
B. Accepting Salazar’s interpretation of
the VPPA would open the door to lawsuits by retail customers who have
never rented, purchased, or subscribed
to any audiovisual content.
Under Salazar’s interpretation, the definition of a
“consumer” under the VPPA is entirely unmoored
from the statute’s focus on audiovisual content. Salazar concedes as much, acknowledging that under his
view “a person who bought” non-audiovisual goods
(such as “candles, sunglasses, posters, and even dog
bandanas”) “would be described as Blockbuster’s ‘consumer.’” Pet’r. Br. 20.
That approach is misguided even when it comes to
traditional video tape service providers like Blockbuster. But it yields especially anomalous results
when extended to retailers and other companies that
aren’t in the audiovisual business.
Indeed, it is not hard to imagine how, under Salazar’s view, the combination of modern website design
and ordinary shopping habits can open the door to potential VPPA claims against retailers:
 A customer is shopping for a t-shirt from a
brick-and-mortar store that does not offer any
audiovisual goods or services.
respondents “use their smartphones when visiting stores
to look up product details or compare prices”).

10
 The same retailer, however, employs digital
video content on its website.
 While browsing t-shirts in the store, the customer pulls out her phone and looks on the retailer’s website for any online discounts.
 While on the retailer’s website, the customer
encounters a video on the website’s home page
showcasing the retailer’s newest line of products.
 Third-party code on the retailer’s website
shares encoded information about the viewing
of the video that is completely indecipherable to
ordinary humans.4
 The customer does not find any discounts on
the website, and she instead purchases a t-shirt
from the store.
Under the proper interpretation of “consumer”
adopted by the Sixth and D.C. Circuits, someone who
buys a t-shirt from a store cannot turn around and sue
a retailer for VPPA statutory damages based on the
retailer’s website. That is because the phrase “goods
and services” is immediately followed by the phrase
“from a video tape service provider.” Pileggi, 146 F.4th
at 1235. As Judge Millett explained, “[t]he named
source ‘from’ which the product must derive gives
meaning to the scope of the regulated goods and

the VPPA near-limitless sweep; on that reading,
whether a person is a “consumer” under the VPPA
would “inexplicably turn[] on purchasing something—
anything—at some however-distant point in time before viewing a video.” Pileggi, 146 F.4th at 1236. According to Salazar, the hypothetical t-shirt purchaser
would become a VPPA “consumer” even though the
purchase would have nothing to do with “obtain[ing]
the products or services that one seeks from a video
tape service provider—that is, videos.” Id. at 1235.5
By encouraging non-video purchasers to bring
VPPA claims, Salazar’s approach would foster further
misuse of the VPPA. In recent years, the VPPA has
been weaponized in this very manner even though
these situations bear no resemblance to the context
that motivated the passage of the statute. Adopting

Salazar’s interpretation will only exacerbate the problem.
II. The Decision Below Correctly Ensures That
The Statutory Definition Of “Consumer”
Performs A Critical Gatekeeping Function
Against Abusive VPPA Litigation.
Salazar’s interpretation of the VPPA’s definition
of “consumer” is not just wrong as a matter of statutory text, context, structure, and purpose; it also will
lead to continued abusive VPPA litigation.
To be sure, courts have dismissed VPPA claims
similar to Salazar’s on other grounds too. For example, while the Second Circuit sided with Salazar on
the meaning of “consumer,” on remand the district
court (after a year of further litigation and motion
practice) dismissed Salazar’s similar claim against
the NBA for failure to allege disclosure of “personally
identifiable information” within the meaning of 18
U.S.C. § 2710(a)(3). Salazar v. Nat’l Basketball Ass’n,
2025 WL 2830939, at *3 (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 6, 2025). A
growing number of courts have likewise dismissed
Pixel-based VPPA claims on that basis. See id. at *3-
5 (citing, e.g., Solomon, 136 F.4th at 54; Hughes v.
Nat’l Football League, 2025 WL 1720295, at *2-3 (2d
Cir. June 20, 2025), cert. denied, 2026 WL 642810
(U.S. Mar. 9, 2026)).
But the next theory that comes along may not be
so susceptible to resolution at the pleadings stage—
and may instead require factual development to determine whether the information allegedly disclosed
qualifies as “personally identifiable information” under the circuit courts’ divergent “interpretation of this
term.” Id. at *3 (describing difference between First
Circuit’s “reasonable foreseeability” standard and

13
Second, Third, and Ninth Circuits’ “ordinary person”
standard).
Because Salazar’s approach forces the terms “personally identifiable information” and “video tape service provider” to bear the entire weight of the VPPA’s
video-privacy aims, it would lead to increased litigation costs, including substantial costs resulting from
discovery. That interpretation not only reflects an unnatural reading of the statute, but threatens to further increase the ability of VPPA class actions to coerce unjustified settlements of even weak claims. See
Smith v. Duffey, 576 F.3d 336, 340 (7th Cir. 2009) (discovery costs alone “can be so steep as to coerce a settlement on terms favorable to the plaintiff even when
his claim is very weak”).
By contrast, adhering to the properly limited definition of “consumer” creates a clear, administrable
line that will be easy to apply at the pleadings stage
in the mine run of cases. A customer who purchases a
t-shirt or a coffee cup from a retailer cannot plausibly
allege (consistent with Rule 11) that she is a renter,
purchaser, or subscriber of audiovisual content.
III. A Properly Limited Definition Of “Consumer” Is Needed To Curb The Recent
Surge Of Abusive VPPA Litigation.
The Court should interpret “consumer” narrowly—and in a manner tethered to the purpose of the
VPPA—for an additional, critical reason: an overlybroad reading of the term will lead to even more vexatious litigation under the statute than what has already taken place over the last several years.

14
A. Claims under the VPPA were infrequent for the first two decades after it
was enacted.
Consistent with the limited purpose animating
the VPPA’s adoption, the VPPA was only rarely invoked in the first twenty years after it was passed. A
review of published opinions available on Westlaw reveals that, from 1988 through 2008, the VPPA was
cited in only 37 opinions. And of those opinions, only
five involved an actual VPPA claim; the remainder of
the opinions cited the VPPA for ancillary purposes.
The five that did involve VPPA claims largely hewed
closely to the context the prompted the passage of the
VPPA. See, e.g., Dirkes v. Borough of Runnemede, 936
F. Supp. 235, 239 (D.N.J. 1996) (“Videos to Go, the
video tape service provider [akin to Blockbuster] in
this matter, violated subsection (b) of the Act by disclosing Plaintiffs’ video rental information to [a police
officer].”).
From 2008 to 2021, there was a slight uptick in
VPPA lawsuits, as online video boomed and certain
plaintiffs and their lawyers began exploring theories
seeking to shift the VPPA from VHS tapes to digital
streaming of audiovisual content.6 Nevertheless,

B. In 2022, businesses, including retailers,
began facing a surge of VPPA class actions.
In recent years, however, some plaintiffs and their
lawyers have attempted “to place a square peg (modern electronic technology) into a round hole (a statute
written in 1988 aimed principally at videotape rental
services).” Yershov v. Gannett Satellite Info. Network,
Inc., 104 F. Supp. 3d 135, 140 (D. Mass. 2015), rev’d
on other grounds, 820 F.3d 482 (1st Cir. 2016).
Specifically, the VPPA litigation landscape
changed dramatically in 2022, when plaintiffs and
their lawyers began targeting countless businesses,
including retailers, with VPPA lawsuits. Many of
these lawsuits are filed by the same firms, using virtually identical complaints, on behalf of a few repeat
named plaintiffs.
Nearly all of these claims are premised on the use
of third-party code, like the Meta Pixel (formerly the
Facebook Pixel), used by many internet businesses for
targeted advertising and other business purposes.

It is no secret why the VPPA is attractive to some

damages or economic harm. In other words, “[w]hat

these suits multiply a minimum . . . statutory

specter of “colossal liability” may force litigants into
“what Judge Friendly called ‘blackmail settlements.’”

Salazar’s sweeping interpretation of the VPPA’s
scope, if adopted, will undoubtedly lead to further coercive lawsuits under the statute.
